item.title: Ribs & Chest Wall — Trigger-Point Pressure Release
clinicalUse: Use when assessment identifies a relevant impairment in Ribs & Chest Wall and the parent technique fits the patient's presentation.
Primary treatment target: rib/chest-wall pain, respiratory movement tolerance and thoracic-linked mobility.
Retain the technique only if it produces a meaningful within-session improvement.
patientPosition: Supported sitting, side-lying or supine/prone depending on the rib level and technique.
Position must allow comfortable breathing throughout.
therapistPosition: Stand beside the involved rib level with hands supported and force kept low.
stabilization: Stabilize the adjacent thorax while respecting normal respiratory excursion.
contact: Use broad contact over the rib or surrounding soft tissue; avoid focal pressure over suspected fracture or vulnerable anterior structures.
Palpate the symptomatic muscle and use a small but comfortable contact over the tender/trigger area.
Confirm that pressure reproduces the patient's familiar local or referred symptoms before treating.
forceDirection: Apply gradually increasing sustained pressure that remains tolerable; do not chase severe pain.
dosage: Commonly 20–60 seconds per point, repeated only if the comparable sign improves.
steps: 1. Record the exact comparable sign for Ribs & Chest Wall: rib/chest-wall pain, respiratory movement tolerance and thoracic-linked mobility.
2. Screen regional red flags, contraindications and technique-specific precautions before touching the patient.
3. Position and stabilize the patient so the target is comfortable and the manual input can be localized.
4. Apply a low-force trial using the parent technique principles and the region-specific contact described above.
5. Monitor pain quality, symptom distribution, guarding and patient confidence throughout.
6. Re-test the original comparable sign immediately after the trial.
7. Keep the technique only when the response is useful, then transfer the gain into active movement, loading or self-management.
reassess: Shoulder or trunk movement linked to symptoms
mistakes: Applying the technique because it is familiar rather than because the examination supports it.
Using more force when the response is unclear or worsening.
Failing to re-test the exact movement or function that justified the treatment.
safety: Do not manually treat unexplained chest pain, dyspnea, suspected rib fracture, acute cardiopulmonary symptoms or systemic illness.
Stop or modify if symptoms peripheralize, neurological status worsens, the response is disproportionate or the patient asks to stop.
item.visualCue: Ribs & Chest Wall assessment → correct regional setup → Trigger-Point Pressure Release → immediate comparable-sign re-test.

subTechniques.name: Pectoralis Major Trigger-Point Pressure Release
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Reduce selected anterior chest/shoulder myofascial pain when it is clearly muscular.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Supine with the arm supported and patient consent/draping maintained.
subTechniques.contact: Broad finger-pad contact over pectoralis major muscle belly away from breast tissue and axillary neurovascular structures.
subTechniques.direction: Apply gentle sustained pressure only if it reproduces familiar muscular symptoms.
subTechniques.reassess: Shoulder horizontal movement, elevation and local tenderness.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: Unexplained chest pain is not a trigger-point diagnosis.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Do not manually treat acute or unexplained cardiopulmonary symptoms.
